title: OSHA State Plans — Overview & How Jurisdiction Works
jurisdiction: There are 22 State Plans covering both private sector and state/local government workers (21 states + Puerto Rico), and 7 State Plans covering state/local government workers only (Connecticut, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and the U.S. Virgin Islands). In the 24 states with no State Plan, federal OSHA covers private employers directly. Every State Plan must be 'at least as effective as' federal OSHA.
adoption_posture: State Plans adopt the federal 1910/1926 standards (identically or with state amendments) and may add state-only standards federal OSHA does not have (heat, ergonomics, workplace violence, right-to-know, etc.).
key_divergences: State Plans can be STRICTER than federal OSHA, never weaker.
Many have unique standards with no federal equivalent (see per-state records).
Some run their own online enforcement portals in addition to the federal one.
penalty_structure: Penalty caps generally track federal OSHA, which adjusts for inflation each January. As of 2025, roughly: Serious / Other-than-Serious up to ~$16,550 each; Willful or Repeat up to ~$165,514 each; Failure-to-Abate ~$16,550 per day. State Plans may set their own schedules but must be 'at least as effective' as federal OSHA.
contractor_impact: A contractor's own crews are covered by whichever authority runs that state (federal OSHA or the State Plan). In the 7 public-sector-only states, PRIVATE contractors stay under FEDERAL OSHA; the state agency only governs government employers (cities, counties, schools, agencies).
notes: Anchor record. Use per-state records for specifics.

title: California — Cal/OSHA (Division of Occupational Safety and Health, DOSH) (State Plan)
agency: Cal/OSHA (Division of Occupational Safety and Health, DOSH)
adoption_posture: Adopts federal standards AND adds numerous California-only standards (Title 8 CCR). The most divergent State Plan in the country.
key_divergences: Injury & Illness Prevention Program (IIPP), T8 §3203 — a written IIPP is MANDATORY for every California employer; no federal equivalent.
Outdoor Heat Illness Prevention, T8 §3395 (shade/water/rest, high-heat procedures at 95F).
Indoor Heat Illness Prevention, T8 §3396 — effective July 23, 2024; applies when indoor temp reaches 82F.
Workplace Violence Prevention Plan, Labor Code 6401.9 (SB 553) — required for most employers since July 1, 2024.
Aerosol Transmissible Diseases, T8 §5199 (healthcare/related).
Permit requirements for trenches 5ft+, certain scaffolds, asbestos, etc.; generally higher penalties and its own citation schedule.
penalty_structure: Penalty caps generally track federal OSHA, which adjusts for inflation each January. As of 2025, roughly: Serious / Other-than-Serious up to ~$16,550 each; Willful or Repeat up to ~$165,514 each; Failure-to-Abate ~$16,550 per day. State Plans may set their own schedules but must be 'at least as effective' as federal OSHA.
contractor_impact: California is a documentation-heavy state: at minimum every client needs a written IIPP, plus heat (indoor+outdoor) and workplace-violence plans. A federal-only program set will fail a Cal/OSHA review.
notes: Signature divergences: IIPP, indoor+outdoor heat, workplace violence, ATD.

key_divergences: Covers state and local government employees only.
penalty_structure: Penalty caps generally track federal OSHA, which adjusts for inflation each January. As of 2025, roughly: Serious / Other-than-Serious up to ~$16,550 each; Willful or Repeat up to ~$165,514 each; Failure-to-Abate ~$16,550 per day. State Plans may set their own schedules but must be 'at least as effective' as federal OSHA.
contractor_impact: Private-sector contractors in this state remain under FEDERAL OSHA — the federal 1910/1926 program set governs your own crews. This agency governs only public employers (cities, counties, school districts, state agencies). It matters if you staff, consult for, or are employed by a government entity here.
